title: ACH vs SWIFT for USD Transfers to India: Costs, Speed, UPI | Grey
summary: ACH cannot reach Indian banks directly, but combined with Grey it beats SWIFT on cost. Compare methods with fees, UPI support, and Indian bank coverage.
body_markdown:
When sending US dollars to India, choosing the right transfer method affects how much your recipient actually receives. India is one of the largest remittance markets in the world, and the difference between a well-chosen and a poorly chosen transfer method can amount to hundreds of dollars per year for regular payments.


This article compares ACH, SWIFT, and FedNow for sending USD to India, explains why ACH alone cannot reach Indian banks, and walks through how Grey handles the transfer, including fees, supported banks, and UPI delivery.


**Also read:**[How to transfer USD from your Indian bank account to a US business partner](https://grey.co/blog/how-to-transfer-usd-from-your-indian-bank-account-to-a-us-business-partner)


## **What is ACH?**


ACH (Automated Clearing House) is a US domestic electronic payment network used for payroll, direct deposits, and contractor payments. ACH is cost-effective (free or under $1 for the sender) and typically settles in 1 to 3 business days.


ACH does not work for sending money directly to India for three reasons: it is a domestic US system only, Indian banks are not part of the ACH network, and ACH does not support currency conversion from USD to INR. To send money to India, you need either a cross-border SWIFT wire or a platform like Grey that handles the conversion and delivery.


## **What is SWIFT?**


SWIFT is the global messaging network used by banks for cross-border payments. It connects over 11,000 financial institutions worldwide, including all major Indian banks: SBI (State Bank of India), HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Axis Bank, Punjab National Bank, Bank of Baroda, and Kotak Mahindra Bank. SWIFT supports sending USD directly to Indian banks, where the receiving bank handles the INR conversion.


SWIFT transfers to India typically take 1 to 5 business days. The costs involve sender fees ($25 to $45), intermediary bank deductions ($15 to $75, variable and unpredictable), and the receiving bank's exchange rate markup (2% to 4% over mid-market is common). For a $3,000 payment, total SWIFT costs can range from $100 to $150.


## **What about FedNow?**


FedNow is the Federal Reserve's instant payment rail. It works only within the US and cannot send money directly to India. However, FedNow can fund a Grey USD account instantly, 24/7/365. From there, Grey handles the transfer to Indian bank accounts or UPI IDs. This two-step approach (instant US-side funding via FedNow, then Grey-to-India delivery) is often faster and cheaper than a traditional SWIFT wire.


## **Why SWIFT is the direct option for India**


If you need to send USD from a US bank directly to an Indian bank, SWIFT is the only direct method. It works with all major Indian banks and handles INR conversion on the receiving end. The drawbacks are unpredictable intermediary fees, slow processing (up to 5 business days), and unfavourable exchange rate markups applied by the receiving bank.


## **The Grey alternative: ACH or FedNow plus India delivery**


Instead of a direct SWIFT wire, you can fund your Grey USD account cheaply via ACH or FedNow, then send from Grey to your recipient's Indian bank account or UPI ID. Grey supports transfers to most major Indian banks, including SBI, HDFC, ICICI, Axis, PNB, Bank of Baroda, and Kotak Mahindra. Grey also supports UPI transfers, which are typically processed within minutes.


This approach gives you transparent pricing: the deposit fee (0.8%, min $2, max $10 for ACH/FedNow) and the conversion fee (1%, capped for certain pairs) are shown before you confirm. No intermediary banks take fees in transit, and you see the exact INR amount your recipient will receive before you send.

## **Tax and regulatory considerations**


[Remittances to India are generally not taxable](https://grey.co/blog/tax-sending-money-india-us) for the sender in the US. However, there are reporting thresholds to be aware of. If your total gifts to a single person exceed the annual gift tax exclusion, you may need to file[IRS Form 709.](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-709)[For FBAR (Report of Foreign Bank and Financial Accounts) purposes](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/report-of-foreign-bank-and-financial-accounts-fbar) , if your foreign financial accounts exceed $10,000 at any point during the year, filing is required. These obligations apply to the sender, not the recipient.


On the receiving side in India, inward remittances for personal support (family maintenance) are generally not taxable for the recipient. Transfers for investment purposes may have different tax implications. Consult a qualified tax advisor for advice specific to your situation.


## **Why the India corridor favours fintech platforms**


India's UPI (Unified Payments Interface) system has made domestic real-time payments the norm. Over 10 billion UPI transactions are processed monthly. This infrastructure means that once USD arrives in India through a platform like Grey and is converted to INR, the final delivery to the recipient's bank account via UPI is nearly instant. The total experience, from the sender confirming the transfer to the recipient seeing INR in their account, is significantly faster than a traditional SWIFT wire.


India's banking system also has well-developed correspondent banking relationships, which historically made SWIFT the default for receiving USD. However, the combination of high SWIFT fees (intermediary deductions, bank markups) and the availability of fintech alternatives has shifted the calculus. For regular payments of $500 to $5,000, the fintech route is almost always cheaper and often faster.


The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) supports inward remittances and has not placed restrictions on receiving foreign currency through licensed platforms. As long as the recipient provides appropriate documentation (KYC and remittance purpose), the transfer process runs smoothly regardless of the platform used.


## **Common mistakes when sending money to India**


Not comparing exchange rates across providers: Indian banks typically apply a 2% to 4% markup on USD-to-INR conversions for SWIFT transfers. Fintech platforms generally offer rates closer to mid-market. On a $5,000 transfer, the difference between a 3% bank markup and a 1% fintech margin is $100.


Sending to the wrong account type: If your recipient has both a savings account and an NRE (Non-Resident External) account, make sure you are sending to the correct one. NRE accounts are designed for non-resident Indians receiving foreign currency, while regular savings accounts may have different processing requirements for inward foreign remittances.


Forgetting about intermediary deductions: SWIFT transfers to India often pass through intermediary banks that deduct fees in transit. A $3,000 payment might arrive as $2,920 or less. The Grey approach eliminates these intermediaries on the US funding side, so you know the exact amount reaching India before you confirm.

## **Frequently asked questions**


### **Can I send ACH payments to India?**


No. ACH only works within the US banking system. Indian banks are not ACH participants. To send USD to India, use SWIFT for a direct bank wire, or fund a Grey account via ACH or FedNow and then transfer from Grey to an Indian bank account or UPI ID.


### **Does Grey support UPI transfers to India?**


Yes. Grey supports sending money to UPI IDs in India. Your recipient receives INR directly to their UPI-linked bank account. UPI transfers are typically processed within minutes.


### **How much does it cost to send USD to India from the US?**


Through Grey, the total cost of $1,000 is approximately $18: a 0.8% deposit fee (capped at $10) plus a 1% conversion fee (capped for certain pairs). A traditional SWIFT wire typically costs $55 to $120 in total fees across sender, intermediary, and receiving banks.


### **Are there tax implications for sending money to India from the US?**


Remittances to India are generally not taxable for the US sender. If total gifts to a single person exceed the annual gift tax exclusion, you may need to file IRS Form 709. For FBAR purposes, if your foreign accounts exceed $10,000 at any point during the year, filing is required. Consult a qualified tax advisor.
